title: A Quarter of the Push, Many Times the Errors

scenes.tts: Robo is a receptor that keeps axons off the midline. So where is the repellent it receives?
scenes.visual: Title card: A Quarter of the Push, Many Times the Errors. Robo receptor on a growth cone, an empty midline beside it, question mark.
scenes.narration: Robo is a receptor that keeps axons off the midline. So where is the repellent it receives?

scenes.tts: In 1999, a run of papers in one issue of the journal Cell named it. It is Slit, a large protein secreted by the midline glia.
scenes.visual: A journal issue with several papers fanned out. Label: 1999, Slit. Midline glia releasing Slit.
scenes.narration: In 1999, a run of papers in one issue of the journal Cell named it. It is Slit, a large protein secreted by the midline glia.

scenes.tts: A companion paper showed that Slit proteins bind Robo receptors.
scenes.visual: Slit binding the first domain of Robo. Small inset of the Slit2 and Robo1 crystal structure. Names on screen: Brose, Bland and colleagues, 1999.
scenes.narration: A companion paper showed that Slit proteins bind Robo receptors.

scenes.tts: Recombinant Slit two repels embryonic spinal motor axons in culture.
scenes.caption: Recombinant Slit2 repels embryonic spinal motor axons in culture.
scenes.visual: Explant in a gel beside Slit cells; axons grow away from the Slit side.
scenes.narration: Recombinant Slit2 repels embryonic spinal motor axons in culture.

scenes.tts: The fly genetics tested the link with flies missing one copy of each gene. Flies missing one copy are called heterozygotes.
scenes.visual: Two chromosomes, one copy of slit and one copy of robo crossed out. Label: heterozygote, slit/+ and robo/+. Names on screen: Kidd, Bland and Goodman.
scenes.narration: The fly genetics tested the link with flies missing one copy of each gene. Flies missing one copy are called heterozygotes.

scenes.tts: Here are made-up numbers in the spirit of that experiment. Score fifty segments per genotype for wrong crossings.
scenes.caption: Here are made-up numbers in the spirit of that experiment. Score 50 segments per genotype for wrong crossings.
scenes.visual: Label: made-up numbers. A strip of 50 segments to be scored.
scenes.narration: Here are made-up numbers in the spirit of that experiment. Score 50 segments per genotype for wrong crossings.

scenes.tts: Missing one copy of slit, two percent of segments go wrong. Missing one copy of robo, four percent.
scenes.caption: Missing one copy of slit, 2 percent of segments go wrong. Missing one copy of robo, 4 percent.
scenes.visual: Bar chart: slit/+ 2 percent; robo/+ 4 percent.
scenes.narration: Missing one copy of slit, 2 percent of segments go wrong. Missing one copy of robo, 4 percent.

scenes.tts: Now remove one copy of each gene. Under a simple independent-error model, you would expect about six percent. What would a much bigger number mean?
scenes.caption: Now remove one copy of each gene. Under a simple independent-error model, you would expect about 6 percent. What would a much bigger number mean?
scenes.visual: Empty third bar labelled slit/+ robo/+, with a dashed line at about 6 percent labelled: independent segment-error null, 1 − 0.98 × 0.96 ≈ 5.9%; negligible baseline.
scenes.narration: Now remove one copy of each gene. Under a simple independent-error model, you would expect about 6 percent. What would a much bigger number mean?

scenes.tts: The made-up result is thirty-two percent. That is far more than the singles together.
scenes.caption: The made-up result is 32 percent. That is far more than the singles together.
scenes.visual: The third bar rises to 32 percent, far above the dashed line.
scenes.narration: The made-up result is 32 percent. That is far more than the singles together.

scenes.tts: Use a toy version of the rule. Count only Robo one, and let each factor scale with gene dose.
scenes.visual: On screen: toy: push = Slit × Robo1; each factor proportional to gene dose; other Robos ignored. Each factor drawn as a bar that halves when a copy is lost.
scenes.narration: Use a toy version of the rule. Count only Robo1, and let each factor scale with gene dose.
scenes.caption: Use a toy version of the rule. Count only Robo1, and let each factor scale with gene dose.

scenes.tts: Then one missing copy leaves half the push. One missing copy of each leaves a quarter.
scenes.visual: Three push levels marked: wild type 1, single heterozygote 1/2, double heterozygote 1/4. Label: toy calculation, not measured signal.
scenes.narration: Then one missing copy leaves half the push. One missing copy of each leaves a quarter.

scenes.tts: Suppose errors simply tracked the push that was lost. Then the double would barely differ from the singles.
scenes.visual: A straight line from lost push to errors. On screen: lost push 1/2 versus 3/4, only 1.5 times as much; errors about 3 percent to about 4.5 percent. The predicted 4.5 percent bar stands beside the observed 32 percent bar.
scenes.narration: Suppose errors simply tracked the push that was lost. Then the double would barely differ from the singles.

scenes.tts: Now add a threshold. Segments vary, so the push varies a little from one segment to the next.
scenes.visual: A steep S-shaped curve with a threshold line; each segment drawn as a small dot with some scatter.
scenes.narration: Now add a threshold. Segments vary, so the push varies a little from one segment to the next.

scenes.tts: With half the push, almost every segment still sits above the threshold. Few fail.
scenes.visual: Dots clustered at push 1/2, nearly all on the safe side of the threshold.
scenes.narration: With half the push, almost every segment still sits above the threshold. Few fail.

scenes.tts: With a quarter, the average push sits near the threshold. Many segments drop below it.
scenes.visual: Dots at push 1/4 straddle the threshold; many turn red.
scenes.narration: With a quarter, the average push sits near the threshold. Many segments drop below it.

scenes.tts: A jump this large points to a genetic interaction. A shared pathway with a threshold explains it simply. These numbers alone cannot prove that model.
scenes.visual: Label: genetic interaction. Below it, smaller: one possible model, a threshold response.
scenes.narration: A jump this large points to a genetic interaction. A shared pathway with a threshold explains it simply. These numbers alone cannot prove that model.

scenes.tts: The binding data and the null mutants say that the process is a ligand acting on a receptor.
scenes.visual: Slit bound to Robo again, with a slit null ladder collapsed beside it.
scenes.narration: The binding data and the null mutants say that the process is a ligand acting on a receptor.

scenes.tts: One puzzle remains. If Slit is Robo's ligand, why do the null mutants look different?
scenes.visual: The robo ladder (thick rungs) beside the slit ladder (collapsed), question mark between them.
scenes.narration: One puzzle remains. If Slit is Robo's ligand, why do the null mutants look different?

scenes.tts: Flies have three Robo receptors. Losing Robo one removes much of the repulsion, so axons cross freely.
scenes.caption: Flies have three Robo receptors. Losing Robo1 removes much of the repulsion, so axons cross freely.
scenes.visual: Growth cone with three receptor types, Robo1, Robo2, Robo3. Small note: fly Robo3 is not the fly version of mouse Robo3. Robo1 fades out.
scenes.narration: Flies have three Robo receptors. Losing Robo1 removes much of the repulsion, so axons cross freely.

scenes.tts: Robo two remains and still hears Slit. So axons are pushed out of the midline, though not kept from crossing back.
scenes.caption: Robo2 remains and still hears Slit. So axons are pushed out of the midline, though not kept from crossing back.
scenes.visual: Robo2 still binds Slit; axons leave the midline but loop back across. Robo3 drawn smaller, off to the side, labelled: positions axons in the rails.
scenes.narration: Robo2 remains and still hears Slit. So axons are pushed out of the midline, though not kept from crossing back.

scenes.tts: Remove Robo one and Robo two together, and the ladder looks much like slit.
scenes.caption: Remove Robo1 and Robo2 together, and the ladder looks much like slit.
scenes.visual: A robo, robo2 double-mutant ladder whose rails collapse toward the midline, beside the slit ladder.
scenes.narration: Remove Robo1 and Robo2 together, and the ladder looks much like slit.

scenes.tts: Losing Slit removes the push through every Robo. Axons at the midline are not pushed out.
scenes.visual: Slit removed; all three receptors idle; axons sit in the midline.
scenes.narration: Losing Slit removes the push through every Robo. Axons at the midline are not pushed out.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: the ligand is shared, and the receptors share the work. Near a threshold, small losses can make large effects.
scenes.visual: Summary card: ligand shared; receptors share the work; a threshold can turn small losses into large effects.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: the ligand is shared, and the receptors share the work. Near a threshold, small losses can make large effects.
